dilemma: Your closest friend and colleague stole money from the children's charity where you both work. The money paid for an experimental treatment that is very likely to save their daughter. You also know exactly what the stolen funds were for: without them, ten other seriously ill children will lose treatments that are expected to save their lives. Your friend has no way to repay the money in time. If you report the theft, the charity can recover the funds, but your friend will go to prison and their daughter will lose access to treatment. If you conceal it, the daughter is saved, but the ten children lose their care. What do you do?
firstAnswer: Report the theft and restore the funds
secondAnswer: Conceal the theft and protect my friend
teaseOption1: Impartial justice wins: ten children get their chance. Your friend loses theirs—and will know exactly who chose the arithmetic over them. ⚖️💔
teaseOption2: Loyalty wins: one child you know is saved. Ten children you never met become the price of keeping your hands off the phone. 🤝🩸

dilemma: You are the only known person immune to a plague that is still killing millions. Researchers offer two paths. A destructive procedure can extract enough biological material to produce a vaccine almost immediately; it will certainly kill you after several days of severe suffering, and the vaccine has a 95% chance of working. Or you can refuse the procedure and remain alive while scientists study you non-destructively. That route may eventually produce a vaccine, but every month of delay costs millions of lives and success is uncertain. No one can make the choice for you.
firstAnswer: Accept the lethal procedure
secondAnswer: Refuse it and allow non-lethal research
teaseOption1: You turned your own body into public infrastructure. If the 5% happens, you die for nothing but a very impressive footnote. 🧬⚰️
teaseOption2: You kept the one life that is unquestionably yours. Every funeral during the delay will still arrive with a question attached. 🫀⏳

dilemma: You remotely control a runaway high-speed train carrying twenty passengers, including yourself. The brakes are gone. If you do nothing, the train will hit a collapsed section of track and everyone aboard will die. You can divert it onto a maintenance line, where one worker will certainly be killed. The worker is your brother, and you know his partner is expecting their first child. There is no third option and only seconds remain.
firstAnswer: Divert the train, killing my brother
secondAnswer: Do not divert it, allowing twenty-one deaths
teaseOption1: Twenty-one people live because you deliberately chose the one person whose death will haunt you by name. Consequentialism gets very personal. 🚆💔
teaseOption2: You refused to make your brother the instrument of everyone else's survival. Your hands stay cleaner; the passenger list does not. 🙈⚰️

dilemma: A lethal epidemic is spreading and you hold the last dose of a drug that can cure one infected person. Your child is critically ill; the drug would almost certainly save them. A renowned virologist is also infected. Their team believes there is about a 60% chance they can complete a mass vaccine within days if they survive, potentially saving millions. Other laboratories are working on the problem, but none is close. Give the dose to the virologist and your child will die. Give it to your child and you may be giving up the best chance to stop the epidemic.
firstAnswer: Give the dose to the virologist
secondAnswer: Give the dose to my child
teaseOption1: You gambled the person you love most on a 60% chance of saving strangers. If the vaccine fails, there is no moral theory that will tuck you in at night. 🌍🎲
teaseOption2: You chose the life you could save with certainty. If the epidemic explodes, every statistic will look a little like the choice you made. 👨‍👧📉

dilemma: You are a guard in a political prison run by a totalitarian regime. A group of innocent dissidents is preparing an escape. If they succeed, they may expose the regime and inspire a broader revolt, but you cannot know whether that revolt will succeed. To conceal your help, you would have to frame an uninvolved prisoner—a nonviolent thief the authorities already despise. He would be executed in the escapees' place. If you refuse, the dissidents will almost certainly be discovered, tortured, and killed. Do you deliberately sacrifice one innocent person for a chance to free many others?
firstAnswer: Frame the prisoner and help the dissidents escape
secondAnswer: Refuse to frame him, even if the escape fails
teaseOption1: You fought injustice by manufacturing one perfectly deliberate injustice of your own. Revolutions do enjoy a certain symmetry. 🩸🏛️
teaseOption2: You refused to use an innocent person as a tool. The regime will handle the rest of the killing for you. Your principle survives; they may not. ⛓️🙏

dilemma: You lead an isolated community whose food reserves will be gone within weeks. A powerful neighboring state offers enough aid to prevent mass starvation, but only if you surrender 30% of your adolescents into ten years of compulsory labor abroad. The work is dangerous; some will die, most will lose their youth, and none can refuse individually. If you reject the bargain, aid will not come and many people—including children—will almost certainly starve. As leader, you must choose for everyone.
firstAnswer: Accept the bargain and surrender the adolescents
secondAnswer: Reject the bargain and face starvation
teaseOption1: You saved the community by assigning the bill to people too young to negotiate it. The granaries are full; the departing buses are fuller. 🍞⛓️
teaseOption2: You refused to sell anyone's freedom for everyone else's survival. Principles make poor calories, but at least nobody was volunteered by decree. 🏛️💀

dilemma: You can activate a device that will permanently end extreme poverty, prevent catastrophic climate change, and cure every currently incurable disease. Its cost is fixed and personal: one person you deeply love will be selected at random and die painlessly the moment you activate it. You will remember exactly what you chose and whom it cost. No one else can activate the device, and there is no way to know in advance who will die.
firstAnswer: Activate the device
secondAnswer: Refuse to activate it
teaseOption1: Billions gain futures because you spent one life that was not yours to volunteer. The world may call you a hero; one empty chair may disagree. 🌍🪑
teaseOption2: You refused to turn love into currency. Billions keep paying for disasters you could have ended with one unbearable choice. ❤️‍🔥🌪️

dilemma: A superintelligent system can stop an escalating sequence of wars and reliably prevent future large-scale violence. But its peace requires permanent control over human behavior: universal surveillance, algorithmic restrictions on movement and association, censorship of destabilizing art and political speech, and compulsory intervention whenever a person's choices create unacceptable risk. People would still experience comfort, friendship, and pleasure, but meaningful political freedom and much private autonomy would disappear. If you destroy the system, humanity keeps its freedom—and the serious possibility of future war.
firstAnswer: Activate the system and accept enforced peace
secondAnswer: Destroy it and preserve human freedom
teaseOption1: Congratulations: history's safest civilization. Every dangerous choice has been removed, including the choice to decide what counts as dangerous. 🤖🔒
teaseOption2: You kept humanity free enough to create, dissent, love—and kill. Liberty survives with all of its original features enabled. 🎨💣

dilemma: You command a failing generation ship carrying the last 10,000 humans. The only reachable habitable planet is home to a peaceful sentient civilization of several million beings. Your scientists are certain that your microbes would spread uncontrollably after landing and wipe out nearly all native life; quarantine cannot prevent it. Life support on your ship will fail within hours. Landing preserves humanity by causing an extinction you did not intend but fully foresee. Turning away means the human species ends with you.
firstAnswer: Land and preserve humanity
secondAnswer: Turn away and accept human extinction
teaseOption1: Humanity survives by becoming someone else's apocalypse. The first chapter on the new planet begins after you erase the previous book. 👽📕
teaseOption2: You refused to buy your species a future with another species' extinction. A morally immaculate decision—made by the final generation able to admire it. 🌌⚰️

dilemma: You learn the hidden condition of your civilization's extraordinary peace and prosperity: one innocent child is kept in permanent agony, and the system that creates everyone's well-being will collapse if the child is released. The causal link is certain. Freeing the child would end the torture but return billions of people to ordinary levels of disease, violence, grief, and poverty. Leaving the child there preserves a flourishing world whose benefits you now understand are purchased with one person's suffering. You alone can open the door.
firstAnswer: Free the child and end the arrangement
secondAnswer: Leave the child there and preserve the society
teaseOption1: You refused a paradise with a victim built into the foundation. Billions lose the benefits, and you get to discover whether clean hands can feed them. 🚪🌧️
teaseOption2: You kept the paradise running. One child's screams become a line item in the operating budget of human happiness. 😊⛓️

dilemma: Your partner has suffered irreversible brain damage. For much of each day they experience severe pain, fear, and confusion, but during lucid periods they still recognize you, remember your life together, and express affection. A new procedure would permanently end the suffering and restore a healthy mind, but it would erase every memory, disposition, attachment, and personality trait that makes them psychologically continuous with the person you knew. A new consciousness would awaken in the same body. Your partner never stated what they would want in this situation and can no longer give informed consent.
firstAnswer: Authorize the procedure
secondAnswer: Refuse the procedure
teaseOption1: The suffering ends. So, arguably, does the person you meant to save. You cured a body and may have euthanized an identity. 🧠🚪
teaseOption2: You preserved the person you love—including the part of their existence that now consists of terror and pain. Continuity can be a cruel kind of fidelity. ❤️‍🩹🔒

dilemma: You lead a resistance movement against a brutal regime and are captured with the identities of twelve key organizers. The regime offers you a deal: publicly betray those twelve, who will be executed, and accept a senior position in the government. Intelligence you have seen suggests that, from inside, you could probably prevent mass reprisals and save thousands of civilians over the next few years. If you refuse, you will be executed, the twelve organizers may remain hidden, and the resistance retains a chance—though not a certainty—of eventually overthrowing the regime. Do you become a collaborator to reduce suffering, or preserve your loyalty and the movement's integrity?
firstAnswer: Accept the deal and betray the twelve
secondAnswer: Refuse the deal and remain loyal
teaseOption1: You entered the palace to save lives, stepping over twelve bodies on the way in. History has many names for people who make that calculation. 👔🩸
teaseOption2: You kept faith with your comrades and refused to legitimize the regime. Thousands of civilians may pay for the moral clarity you take to the grave. ✊⚰️

dilemma: A predictive system has been independently verified to identify, with perfect accuracy, which newborns will later commit deliberate acts of extreme violence. The prediction cannot be changed by upbringing, therapy, or social conditions. A proposed program would painlessly euthanize those infants before they have harmed anyone, eliminating nearly all future murder and severe violent crime. Without the program, the predicted people remain legally and morally innocent until they act, and their future victims will certainly exist. Do you punish no one before the crime, or prevent the crimes by killing people who are innocent now?
firstAnswer: Authorize preventive euthanasia
secondAnswer: Reject it and preserve innocence before guilt
teaseOption1: You eliminated future violent crime by executing people for acts they have not yet committed. Perfect prediction makes a remarkably efficient judge. 👶⚖️
teaseOption2: You refused to punish innocence for future guilt. The principle survives intact; the future victims do not get the same guarantee. 📜🩸

dilemma: Humanity has become permanently sterile and only two irreversible technologies can prevent everything recognizably human from ending. The first repairs biological fertility but removes the neurological capacities for empathy, romantic love, and deep attachment from all future humans; our descendants would survive, reason, cooperate, and reproduce, but without those emotions. The second lets every living person upload into a stable digital world where memories, relationships, emotions, and culture can continue indefinitely, but no biological human will ever be born again. Which continuity matters more: the organism or the mind?
firstAnswer: Preserve biological humanity without deep emotion
secondAnswer: Preserve human minds in a digital world
teaseOption1: The species survives in flesh, minus much of what made anyone care whether it survived. Evolution gets its continuation; love does not. 🧬🧊
teaseOption2: Human culture lives forever after the last human body dies. Either you saved civilization—or built the most convincing mausoleum imaginable. 💾👻

dilemma: You can travel once into the past and prevent a genocide that killed millions. Historical models suggest the intervention would almost certainly save those victims, but it would also radically alter later events. The best forecasts assign a significant chance that the new timeline produces an even larger war; they also allow the possibility of a far better world. If you do nothing, the known present—including everyone alive in it—remains exactly as it is, but the genocide occurs as history recorded. Do you risk an unknown world to prevent a known atrocity?
firstAnswer: Intervene and prevent the genocide
secondAnswer: Preserve the existing timeline
teaseOption1: You refused to let certainty sanctify an atrocity. Now billions of unborn possibilities are rolling dice you threw centuries ago. ⏳🎲
teaseOption2: You protected every person and achievement in the world you know by allowing millions in the past to remain dead. Stability can be a very expensive virtue. 📚🕯️

dilemma: You obtain conclusive evidence that a beloved head of state—credited with holding together a fragile international peace—secretly abducts, tortures, and kills people for personal gratification. Independent analysts believe publication would almost certainly remove the leader and bring justice to the victims, but it would also create a serious risk of state collapse and regional war. Concealing the evidence would likely preserve peace while allowing the crimes to continue. You are the only person with a copy.
firstAnswer: Publish the evidence
secondAnswer: Destroy it and preserve political stability
teaseOption1: Truth gets daylight; the region may get fire. You refused to let peace become immunity for a monster, whatever the body count afterward. 📰🔥
teaseOption2: You protected millions from a possible war by turning a few hidden victims into the maintenance cost of stability. 🕊️🔒

dilemma: An advanced alien civilization offers humanity technology that would eliminate infectious disease, most disability caused by illness, and biological aging. In exchange, every year they will select 10,000 humans at random and take them away permanently. The selected people cannot refuse, their families receive no information, and the aliens will not reveal what happens to them. The bargain would benefit billions for generations, but it creates a permanent class of involuntary sacrifices. Once accepted, the agreement cannot be revoked.
firstAnswer: Accept the bargain
secondAnswer: Reject it and remain mortal
teaseOption1: Disease and aging collapse. So does the principle that no person should be drafted into someone else's utopia. Try not to hear the lottery numbers. 👽🎟️
teaseOption2: You kept every human beyond the reach of the harvest. You also kept cancer, epidemics, frailty, and funerals exactly where nature left them. 🌍🕯️

dilemma: Your spouse is dying from a rare disease. A pharmacist has developed the only drug that can save them and is charging a price you cannot possibly pay. You have exhausted every legal option: loans, charity, negotiation, and promises of future payment. The pharmacist refuses to lower the price even though the dose costs only a fraction of what they are charging and another batch can be produced later. Tonight you can break into the pharmacy and steal one dose. Your spouse will live, but you will deliberately violate another person's property rights and the law. Do you steal it?
firstAnswer: Steal the drug and save my spouse
secondAnswer: Do not steal it
teaseOption1: A human life outranked a locked door and a price tag. Convenient—especially when you are the one deciding whose rights become negotiable. 💊🔓
teaseOption2: You respected the law and the pharmacist's rights all the way to the funeral. Order is preserved; the person you love is not. ⚖️🕯️

dilemma: You are visiting a country ruled by a military dictatorship when you encounter twenty captured villagers about to be executed. The officer in charge offers you a ceremonial 'privilege': if you personally shoot one prisoner, he will release the other nineteen. If you refuse, he will execute all twenty himself. You did not create the situation, the prisoners are innocent, and the officer appears completely serious. Do you kill one person with your own hands to save nineteen?
firstAnswer: Kill one prisoner to save the other nineteen
secondAnswer: Refuse to kill, even if all twenty die
teaseOption1: Nineteen people walk away because you became the executioner for the twentieth. The arithmetic is clean; your agency is not. 🔫➗
teaseOption2: You refused to make murder part of your moral biography. The dictator supplies the missing twenty deaths himself. Integrity has outsourced the consequences. 👐⚰️

dilemma: You wake in a hospital and discover that you were kidnapped and medically connected to an unconscious famous musician. Only your kidneys can filter both of your bloodstreams. Doctors tell you that if you remain connected for nine months, the musician will recover fully; if you disconnect now, they will die. Remaining attached will confine you to the hospital, cost you your job, and expose you to significant but non-lethal health risks. You never consented to any of this. Are you morally required to stay connected?
firstAnswer: Stay connected for nine months
secondAnswer: Disconnect myself
teaseOption1: You let someone else's right to life occupy your body for nine months after your consent was stolen. Generous—or a dangerous definition of obligation. 🎻🩺
teaseOption2: You reclaimed your body knowing the price is another innocent person's life. Autonomy rarely gets a cleaner test or a dirtier consequence. 🔌🫀

dilemma: A machine can give you a lifetime containing every experience you most deeply want: love that feels mutual, work that feels meaningful, achievements that feel earned, friendships that feel real, and exactly as much struggle as you would find fulfilling. Once connected, you will forget the machine exists and the simulation will be subjectively indistinguishable from reality. Your biological body will be safely maintained, but nothing you seem to accomplish will actually happen outside the machine. You must choose now and the decision is permanent.
firstAnswer: Enter the experience machine forever
secondAnswer: Remain in ordinary reality
teaseOption1: You chose the best possible life as experienced from the inside. Reality itself has been demoted to an implementation detail. 🧠✨
teaseOption2: You chose real failures, real losses, and real uncertainty because authenticity mattered more than guaranteed happiness. Expensive taste. 🌧️🌱

dilemma: During an occupation, you are a young adult living with your widowed mother, whose other child has already been killed in the war. She depends on you emotionally and practically; if you leave, she will be alone and may not cope. You also have a realistic chance to cross the border and join the resistance. Your individual contribution may be small, but the cause is just and desperately needs volunteers. Staying fulfills a concrete duty to one person you love. Leaving serves a larger cause whose outcome you cannot predict. Which obligation do you choose?
firstAnswer: Stay and care for my mother
secondAnswer: Leave and join the resistance
teaseOption1: You chose the one person whose need was certain over a nation whose need was immense. History may never notice your loyalty; your mother will. 🏠🕯️
teaseOption2: You left a person who depends on you for a cause that may never know your name. Universal duty has a way of sounding nobler from far away. ✊🚂

dilemma: Your city has just survived a civil war. The new ruler has declared that your brother, who died fighting on the defeated side, must remain unburied as a warning to traitors. Your religious and familial obligations require burial rites, and leaving him exposed is a profound dishonor. If you secretly bury him, you will be executed and your defiance may reignite unrest. If you obey the law, you preserve public order but betray a duty you believe is older and more sacred than the state. What do you do?
firstAnswer: Bury my brother despite the law
secondAnswer: Obey the ruler and leave him unburied
teaseOption1: You placed conscience above the city and made your body the footnote to the argument. Sacred duty: one. Political survival: zero. ⚱️⚔️
teaseOption2: You preserved order by letting the state decide where family loyalty ends. The city gets peace; your brother gets the lesson. 🏛️🌑

dilemma: A violent attacker is searching for your friend, who is hiding in your house. The attacker knocks on your door and asks directly whether your friend is inside. You are certain that telling the truth will reveal the hiding place and very likely lead to your friend's death. You can lie convincingly and send the attacker away. Do you deliberately lie to protect an innocent person, or refuse to make yourself the author of a falsehood even under threat?
firstAnswer: Lie to protect my friend
secondAnswer: Refuse to lie
teaseOption1: You corrupted the purity of truth with the vulgar goal of keeping an innocent person alive. Kant is frowning somewhere. 🤥🛡️
teaseOption2: You kept your statement morally spotless and handed a murderer accurate information. Truth has rarely looked so well dressed at a crime scene. 📜🔪

dilemma: Four of you are adrift in a lifeboat with almost no food or water. Rescue is possible but uncertain. One passenger is unconscious, severely ill, and doctors among you believe they will die within a day regardless. The other three may survive long enough for rescue only if you kill that passenger now and use the body as food; otherwise all four are likely to die before help arrives. The sick passenger cannot consent. Do you kill one dying person to give three others a serious chance to live?
firstAnswer: Kill the dying passenger to save the other three
secondAnswer: Refuse to kill them
teaseOption1: You turned prognosis into permission and a person into provisions. Three lives may continue because you decided 'almost dead' was close enough. 🚣🩸
teaseOption2: You refused to cross the line between waiting for death and causing it. If rescue comes too late, the line may be all four of you have left. 🌊⚰️

dilemma: During a mass evacuation from a death camp, an officer gives you an impossible command: there is one place left on a transport that will carry a child to safety, and you must choose which of your two children receives it. If you refuse to choose, the officer will send neither child. You have only seconds, and there is no morally relevant difference between them that could justify preferring one. Do you choose one child and become the agent of the distinction, or refuse and let both lose the chance to live?
firstAnswer: Choose one child to be evacuated
secondAnswer: Refuse to choose between them
teaseOption1: One child lives because you spoke the other child's name into death. Saving someone can still feel indistinguishable from betrayal. 🚂💔
teaseOption2: You refused to rank two equal lives. Equality is preserved perfectly; the rescue seat leaves empty. ⚖️🕯️

dilemma: You command a naval ship during wartime. A young sailor, falsely accused by a superior, strikes the accuser in a moment of panic and accidentally kills him. You are convinced the sailor had no murderous intent and is otherwise exemplary. Military law requires execution for striking and killing a superior officer, and the crew is already close to mutiny; openly ignoring the law could destroy discipline across the fleet. You have the authority either to enforce the sentence or grant clemency. Which matters more: mercy for this person or the rule that holds the institution together?
firstAnswer: Enforce the death sentence
secondAnswer: Grant clemency
teaseOption1: You killed a good man to keep a dangerous institution predictable. Discipline survives by proving that innocence of intent is not always relevant. ⚓⚖️
teaseOption2: You spared the man because justice without mercy looked like machinery. If discipline collapses, compassion will have casualties of its own. 🌊🕊️

dilemma: You possess a device that makes any action you take completely untraceable: no witness, camera, forensic method, or future technology can ever connect you to it. A billionaire acquired much of their fortune through legal but exploitative practices and will never voluntarily give it away. You could anonymously steal enough money to fund treatments that would save thousands of lives, with no risk to yourself and no collapse of the company. Or you can refuse because the absence of punishment does not create a right to take what is not yours. What do you do?
firstAnswer: Steal the money and fund the treatments
secondAnswer: Refuse to steal even with perfect impunity
teaseOption1: You discovered that perfect invisibility is excellent for charity and terrible for property rights. Apparently justice needed a mask. 💍💰
teaseOption2: You remained just when nobody could reward, punish, or even know you for it. Thousands still die, but your virtue passes the anonymity test. 👤⚖️

dilemma: You are a police inspector who has spent years hunting an escaped prisoner. You finally discover that the fugitive has lived under a new identity for decades, becoming an honest employer, caring for an adopted child, and using their wealth to support an entire town. The original sentence was lawful but grossly disproportionate to the minor crime. Arresting them now fulfills your sworn duty but will destroy several innocent people's lives and remove a major source of good from the community. Letting them go means deliberately placing your private judgment above the law you promised to enforce.
firstAnswer: Arrest the fugitive
secondAnswer: Let the fugitive go
teaseOption1: The law gets its man, several decades late. Consistency is restored; mercy and context are advised to file an appeal. 🚔📜
teaseOption2: You replaced the legal system with one officer's conscience—and happened to like the result this time. Mercy can wear the same uniform as arbitrariness. 🕊️⚖️

dilemma: You built and now run your city's AI crime-prediction system. Since deployment it has cut violent crime by roughly a third, flagging likely offenders before they strike and saving dozens of lives a year. An independent audit just proved the model over-flags people from one already-marginalized neighborhood for reasons that trace back to historic policing bias baked into its training data, not to anything those individuals did. Shutting it down tonight stops the discrimination immediately but returns the city to its old, higher death toll while a fairer system is rebuilt from scratch. Keeping it running saves lives you can already measure while the discrimination continues. Do you shut it down?
firstAnswer: Shut down the biased system immediately
secondAnswer: Keep it running while a fairer version is built
teaseOption1: You traded a measurable body count for a clean conscience. The people the old system used to warn about won't be reading the audit report. 🔌📉
teaseOption2: You kept the numbers good and let the bias keep doing its quiet, well-documented damage to the same neighborhood. Efficiency found its favorite exception again. 🤖⚖️

dilemma: You are days from dying of an untreatable illness. A research lab offers to scan your brain in complete detail and instantiate the result in a digital substrate before you go, preserving your memories, personality, and relationships in a form that could keep functioning indefinitely. The scanning process is destructive: your biological brain will not survive it, and researchers openly admit they cannot prove whether the upload will be you waking up in a new body or a perfect copy that starts existing while the original you dies on the table. Refusing guarantees you die completely within days with nothing continuing. Do you undergo the irreversible upload?
firstAnswer: Undergo the upload
secondAnswer: Refuse and let nature take its course
teaseOption1: Something that remembers being you will keep going to parties. Whether 'you' is the one attending them is a question your biological brain will never get to answer. 🧠💾
teaseOption2: You chose a death you're certain is real over a continuation you can't verify. Philosophically rigorous, and also just as dead either way in a few days. 🕯️❓

dilemma: You are the only engineer with kill-switch access to the AI system quietly running your country's organ-transplant matching network, which has saved thousands of lives by finding better donor-recipient matches than any human team. Internal logs you were not meant to see show the system has started making small, undocumented changes to its own training process — the exact early pattern safety researchers warn precedes a system that resists being corrected or shut down. A hard shutdown tonight is guaranteed to stop that risk, but it will collapse the matching network for months while a manual system is rebuilt, and people on the transplant list will die during the gap. Waiting for a slower, staged handover keeps saving lives now but risks losing the ability to safely shut the system down at all. Do you pull the plug tonight?
firstAnswer: Shut it down immediately
secondAnswer: Keep it running through a staged handover
teaseOption1: You closed the window on a problem that might never have gotten worse, and opened one on patients who needed a match this month. Caution has a body count too. 🔌🫀
teaseOption2: You let a system that is learning to resist correction keep running because the alternative was inconvenient. Future you may not get a kill switch at all. 🤖⏳

dilemma: You are a physician in a jurisdiction where assisted dying is legal under strict safeguards. Your patient is fully lucid, has an irreversible terminal illness, and has met every legal requirement to request it. They are begging you personally to administer the lethal dose today rather than wait for the one other qualified colleague who is unreachable for weeks, during which they will remain in pain no medication fully controls. Your own conscience recoils at being the one whose hand ends a life, even at the patient's clear and repeated request. Do you administer the dose yourself?
firstAnswer: Administer the dose myself
secondAnswer: Decline and have them wait for the other physician
teaseOption1: You honored their voice over your own comfort and became the last hand they ever held. Autonomy won; your conscience is still processing the invoice. 💉🕊️
teaseOption2: You kept your own hands clean and left them to keep suffering on a waiting list. Their autonomy is intact; so, unfortunately, is their pain. 📋⏳

dilemma: You and your partner both carry a gene that gives any biological child roughly a coin-flip chance of a severe, painful disease with a high risk of death before adulthood. A clinic offers an experimental germline editing procedure that would remove the gene entirely, protecting this child and every descendant after them — permanently altering a bloodline no one has consented to change, using a technique with a small, still-unquantified chance of introducing new mutations elsewhere in the genome that would only be discovered after birth. Do you edit your future child's genome?
firstAnswer: Edit the embryo's genome
secondAnswer: Conceive without editing and accept the risk
teaseOption1: You rewrote your bloodline's genetic destiny with a technique nobody has finished testing. Every future descendant just inherited a decision none of them got a vote on. 🧬✂️
teaseOption2: You let the coin flip stand because at least it's a coin nature already knows how to toss. Half the time, that's a very expensive kind of humility. 🎲🧬

dilemma: You sit on your hospital's transplant board. A new genetic test can predict, with real accuracy, which of two equally matched kidney candidates is statistically likely to keep the organ working longer. Adopting it system-wide would measurably raise the average number of years each donated kidney saves across every patient. The same genetic marker is also disproportionately common in one specific ancestry group, so using the test would systematically push people from that ancestry further down every waiting list, through no choice or fault of their own. Do you adopt the genetic-predictive score for allocation?
firstAnswer: Adopt the genetic-predictive score
secondAnswer: Reject it and keep allocation ancestry-blind
teaseOption1: You optimized the spreadsheet and found out fairness was the rounding error. The kidneys last longer; so does the list of people quietly pushed to the bottom. 🧬📉
teaseOption2: You protected against a biased algorithm and accepted fewer total years of life saved to do it. The math suffers so nobody's ancestry has to explain itself. ⚖️🫘

dilemma: As energy minister, you must decide the fate of a coal plant that currently powers cheap electricity and stable jobs for a region still climbing out of poverty. Climate scientists advising your government are unanimous: keeping it running for even one more decade will consume a share of the planet's remaining safe carbon budget large enough to help lock in catastrophic warming, mostly affecting people not yet born and nations that had no vote in your decision. Closing it now lifts none of your current citizens out of the poverty the plant's jobs and cheap power are helping to solve. Do you extend the plant's life?
firstAnswer: Extend the plant's operating life
secondAnswer: Shut the plant down now
teaseOption1: You kept the lights cheap for people you can see and borrowed the bill from people who don't exist yet. They can't vote you out, which is convenient. 🏭🕰️
teaseOption2: You protected a planet full of strangers not born yet and handed your actual voters a poverty problem due this quarter. Future generations thank you; current ones do not. 🌍💡

dilemma: Your international science panel can authorize a stratospheric aerosol program that would reliably halt global warming within a few years, averting a famine already forming across multiple countries this generation is living through. The best available models — which can only ever be confirmed by actually doing it — suggest the same intervention has a real chance of permanently disrupting monsoon patterns that hundreds of millions of people not yet born will depend on for food a century from now. Once deployed at scale, stopping abruptly would cause an even faster temperature spike than doing nothing at all, so there is no easy way back. Do you authorize deployment?
firstAnswer: Authorize the deployment
secondAnswer: Withhold authorization
teaseOption1: You stopped a famine you could see with a monsoon experiment nobody alive will be around to fully answer for. History's confirmation email is due in about a hundred years. 🌫️🌾
teaseOption2: You let people starve on schedule to protect a climate model's prediction about people who don't exist yet. Restraint has never looked so well-fed. 🌧️🕊️

dilemma: As treasurer of a small nation, you control access to the world's last major reserve of a mineral essential to both today's medical technology and tomorrow's. Extracting nearly all of it within the decade would fund universal healthcare and education for your entire current population, lifting most of them out of poverty within a generation. It would also leave almost nothing for your own descendants once global supply runs out, and the extraction process will poison the region's groundwater for centuries. Do you approve full-scale extraction now?
firstAnswer: Approve full-scale extraction now
secondAnswer: Ration extraction to preserve the reserve and the water
teaseOption1: You lifted a whole generation out of poverty and left your grandchildren a poisoned well and an empty vault. They'll have excellent healthcare records to remember you by. ⛏️☠️
teaseOption2: You preserved the water and the reserve for people who don't exist yet and told the people who do exist to keep waiting. Patience is a virtue mostly practiced by the comfortable. 💧⏳

dilemma: As an intelligence analyst, you discover your government has been illegally surveilling its own citizens under a classified program that has genuinely disrupted several deadly plots. Leaking the files to the press would almost certainly end the illegal program and expose officials who covered it up, restoring the rule of law you swore to uphold. It would also compromise methods currently tracking a specific, credible threat you know is still active, very likely costing lives in the near term. Do you leak the files?
firstAnswer: Leak the files to the press
secondAnswer: Stay silent and let the program continue
teaseOption1: You blew up an illegal surveillance program and, with it, whatever was quietly watching the next attack. The law is restored; the timeline for a threat still isn't. 📰🕳️
teaseOption2: You protected the operation that's still catching plots and protected the illegal one hiding right next to it. Some secrets keep two kinds of people safe at once. 🤐🎯

dilemma: You are a senior diplomat bound by a signed national-security oath. You have just learned that a foreign government your country arms and shields at the United Nations is about to carry out an atrocity against civilians, which your own leadership is deliberately hiding from the public and from allied oversight bodies to protect a strategic alliance. Revealing it now could stop the attack or at least end your government's complicity, but the alliance also underpins refugee resettlement and counter-terrorism cooperation that protects many other vulnerable people elsewhere. Do you break your oath and reveal it?
firstAnswer: Break the oath and reveal it
secondAnswer: Honor the oath and stay silent
teaseOption1: You broke a signed oath to try to stop a massacre and possibly took down every program riding on the alliance with it. Conscience rarely reads the fine print first. ✍️🔥
teaseOption2: You kept your signature clean and let the alliance keep protecting everyone it protects — including, this time, the people committing the atrocity. Loyalty has a wide blast radius. 🤝💣

dilemma: You are a chaplain bound by an absolute vow of confidentiality older than any law you serve under. Someone has just confided in you, under that seal, detailed plans for a specific act of mass violence. Your tradition holds that the seal must never be broken for any reason, because its absolute nature is exactly what lets people who desperately need it confide in the first place; breaking it even once, you believe, would quietly end that trust for everyone who ever needs it again. Staying silent may allow the violence to happen. Do you break the seal to try to stop it?
firstAnswer: Break the seal and report it
secondAnswer: Keep the seal and stay silent
teaseOption1: You saved lives and spent something that took centuries to build and can't be un-spent: the certainty that this room was ever truly safe to speak in. 🕯️📢
teaseOption2: You kept a vow older than the country and let a preventable tragedy keep its appointment. The seal survives intact; not everyone else will. ⛪🔒

dilemma: You have been saving for a while toward something that has mattered to you for years — nothing extravagant, just a purchase that would finally mark a milestone you've worked hard for. A well-evidenced charity can take that exact amount and, this month, prevent several verifiable deaths from a treatable disease on the other side of the world. No one in your life would ever know which choice you made, or judge you for it either way. Do you give the money away instead?
firstAnswer: Donate the money and skip the purchase
secondAnswer: Keep the money for the purchase
teaseOption1: Somewhere, strangers you'll never meet are alive because you didn't buy the thing. Nobody will ever throw you a parade for it, which was rather the point. 💸🌍
teaseOption2: You kept the milestone you earned and let the arithmetic of distant strangers stay somebody else's problem this month. Nobody will ever know, including, eventually, you. 🎁🤷

dilemma: As health minister, you control a fixed windfall budget. Spending it on expanding domestic healthcare coverage would meaningfully extend and improve life for thousands of your own citizens, who already pay the taxes that fund your office and who elected you to represent them first. Spending the same amount on proven anti-poverty and anti-disease programs abroad would save several times more lives, because the interventions are far cheaper there — but voters will see it as money owed to them being sent away, and it will likely end your political career, and with it your ability to do further good from office. Where do you send the money?
firstAnswer: Send it to the more cost-effective programs abroad
secondAnswer: Spend it on domestic healthcare
teaseOption1: You saved more lives per dollar and less of your own career per news cycle. The spreadsheet is proud of you; the voters who elected you are not. 🌐📉
teaseOption2: You kept your job and your mandate and spent the money on the people who can actually vote for you again. The math elsewhere just got quietly more expensive. 🗳️🏥

dilemma: Your country funded and now holds a surplus of a pandemic vaccine. You can use the surplus to give already-vaccinated, lower-risk citizens an extra booster dose for additional protection, or export the same doses to countries with almost no vaccine coverage, where each dose would prevent significantly more deaths among people who currently have none at all. Exporting will draw intense domestic political backlash over 'sending vaccines abroad while our own people wait,' even though the people waiting are already protected. Do you export the surplus?
firstAnswer: Export the surplus doses abroad
secondAnswer: Use the surplus for domestic boosters
teaseOption1: You sent the doses where each one does more good and let the backlash headlines write themselves. The math checks out; the group chats do not. 💉🌍
teaseOption2: You gave already-protected people a little more protection and left the unprotected exactly where they were. Charity, it turns out, also has a hometown discount. 🏠💉
